title: Predicting 28-day and 90-day mortality in microbiologically-confirmed sepsis: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Sepsis patients with confirmed microbial infection represent a clinically important subgroup requiring specialized prognostic tools, though existing models fail to address their unique characteristics. A retrospective analysis was conducted using the MIMIC-IV repository, selecting adult sepsis cases fulfilling sepsis-3.0 criteria with microbiological confirmation. Primary endpoints were 28- and 90-day all-cause mortality. Analytical approaches included nonparametric comparative tests, stepwise survival regression modeling, and comprehensive sensitivity evaluations. Our analysis encompassed 5,694 patients with culture-confirmed sepsis, demonstrating mortality rates of 15.8% (28-day) and 17.5% (90-day), respectively. Multivariable regression identified significant mortality predictors (all p < 0.001), including age, respiratory rate, hemoglobin, lactate levels, vasoactive drug use, CCI, LODS score, SIRS score, SAPS III, and OASIS. These variables were incorporated into model 2 and model 4, both of which demonstrated strong predictive performance for 28-day and 90-day mortality with model 2 (AUC: 0.798; specificity: 0.765; sensitivity: 0.678) and model 4 (AUC: 0.795; specificity: 0.730; sensitivity: 0.708). Both models demonstrated consistent predictive performance in subgroup analyses. However, no significant association was observed between infection site, pathogenic microorganism type, and patient prognosis (p ≥ 0.05). These findings establish clinically applicable risk stratification tools specifically designed for culture-positive sepsis, potentially enabling more tailored therapeutic decisions for this vulnerable patient cohort. Not applicable.
full_text:
Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection [1]. Studies report that mortality rates remain high, with an average 30-day septic shock mortality of 34.7%, 90-day septic shock mortality of 38.5%, and 90-day sepsis mortality of 32.2% [2]. Consistent with this, multiple studies confirm persistently elevated mortality in sepsis patients [3–5]. Consequently, sepsis carries a poor prognosis with sustained high mortality rates. Sepsis is a heterogeneous disease [6]. According to the latest Sepsis-3.0 definition, sepsis patients include those with confirmed pathogenic microbial infections as well as those with suspected infections but without detected pathogens [1]. Numerous studies have identified pathogenic microorganisms—particularly Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa—as key contributors to infection and elevated mortality [7–9]. Consequently, pathogen-positive sepsis patients are likely to face higher mortality rates and poorer prognoses. This subgroup warrants special clinical attention. However, large cohort studies focusing on pathogen-positive sepsis patients remain scarce. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the clinical characteristics and prognosis of pathogen-positive sepsis, establish a prognostic model for risk assessment, and facilitate early intervention to reduce sepsis-related mortality. This retrospective study analyzed adult patients (> 18 years) from the MIMIC-IV v2.2 database (2008–2019) who met sepsis-3.0 criteria (SOFA score ≥ 2 with suspected infection) and had microbiologically confirmed infections (positive bacterial/fungal cultures). In this study utilizing the MIMIC-IV database, culture positivity was strictly defined by clinically significant microbial growth from either sterile sites (blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or sterile body fluids) or non-sterile sites (sputum, urine, or wound cultures) when accompanied by compatible clinical symptoms and subsequent targeted antimicrobial therapy. The database records include standardized culture durations (5 days for bacteria and 30 days for fungi), in accordance with the clinical laboratory protocols at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. Suspected infection required both antibiotic administration (> 48 h) and microbiological culture orders. Only patients with an anticipated ICU survival exceeding 24 h after admission were included. Exclusion criteria comprised culture-negative cases, inter-ICU transfers, incomplete records (missing critical variables such as worst 24-hour ICU vitals/labs), and non-index ICU admissions. The population was obtained from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC IV 2.2) database [10]. The MIMIC IV2.2 database is from populations from 2008 to 2019. The MIMIC-IV database is a publicly available, de-identified critical care dataset from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), containing comprehensive clinical data for over 40,000 ICU patients. The number of patients with a diagnosis of sepsis 3.0 was 25,597, of which 5,694 were sepsis patients who were positive for pathogenic microorganisms. The MIMIC IV v2.2 was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (2001-P001699/14) and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (No. 0403000206). All data were fully de-identified in compliance with ethical regulations, and institutional review board approval was obtained with a waiver of informed consent due to the retrospective use of anonymized records. All studies are based on the Declaration of Helsinki. In this study, we collected baseline data from sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms, including demographic characteristics (age, gender, and comorbidities), infection-related details (site of infection and pathogen species), worst vital signs and laboratory test values within the first 24 h of ICU admission, and prognostic indicators such as vasoactive drug treatment, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), hospitalization duration, ICU length of stay, 28-day mortality, and 90-day mortality. Disease severity was assessed using multiple scoring systems using the worst values within 24 h of ICU admission: the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II) and III, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Logistic Organ Dysfunction System (LODS) score, Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (OASIS), and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria. All continuous variables in this study were skewed and thus presented as the interquartile range (IQR). Group comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables and Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified risk factors associated with 28-day and 90-day mortality in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms. Prognostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement(NRI) along with sensitivity and specificity measures. We employed DeLong’s test to statistically compare the area under the curve (AUC) values between the two models. While our study utilized the entire available cohort from the MIMIC-IV database, we performed a post hoc power calculation based on published literature for similar sepsis prognosis studies. A prior study [11] examining mortality predictors in sepsis reported effect sizes ranging from 1.3 to 2.0 for key variables, including age, organ dysfunction scores, and laboratory markers. Assuming similar effect sizes, a power analysis with α = 0.05 and power = 80% indicated that a minimum sample of 1,200-1,500 patients would be required to detect these clinically meaningful associations. Our final cohort of 5,694 patients, therefore, provides more than adequate power to identify significant predictors while accounting for potential confounders. This sample size also comfortably exceeds the recommended 10–20 events per variable for Cox regression analyses, ensuring robust model development without overfitting. For variables with less than 20% missingness, we employed multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) using predictive mean matching, incorporating all model covariates and outcomes in the imputation model to preserve underlying relationships. Continuous variables were imputed using truncated regression to prevent biologically implausible values, while categorical variables used logistic regression. 25,597 patients met the Sepsis 3.0 diagnostic criteria. We excluded 19,903 culture-negative cases and 1,067 cases with incomplete records or ICU transfers, resulting in the final cohort of 5,694 culture-positive sepsis patients analyzed in our study. Table 1 presents baseline data for 28-day mortality prognosis in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms. Compared to the survival group, non-survivors were older, had higher rates of chronic kidney disease, and exhibited significantly worse clinical parameters: faster respiratory and heart rates; lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure; reduced arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2), platelet counts, hemoglobin, and calcium levels; and elevated prothrombin time (PT), international normalized ratio (INR), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), glucose, lactate, and potassium levels. The 28-day and 90-day mortality rates in sepsis patients with pathogenic microbiota positivity were 15.8% and 17.5%, respectively. Age, respiratory rate, hemoglobin levels, lactate levels, use of vasoactive drugs, Charlson Comorbidity Index, LODS, OASIS, SIRS, and SAPS III scores were all independent risk factors for both 28-day and 90-day mortality in this patient group (p < 0.001). Additionally, OASIS was specifically identified as an independent risk factor for 28-day mortality. Several studies have reported that sepsis is associated with high morbidity and mortality [4, 11, 12]. This study found that the short-term and long-term mortality rates among patients with sepsis and confirmed pathogenic microorganisms were approximately 20%. Both previous research and this study highlight that sepsis continues to carry a high mortality risk, particularly in patients with microbiologically confirmed infections. However, this study did not identify specific high-mortality pathogenic microorganisms as independent predictors of short- or long-term mortality in this patient population. Instead, mortality may be attributed to multisystem organ damage resulting from the dysregulated inflammatory response triggered by these pathogens. Given these findings, further investigation into multisystem injury patterns and prognostic scoring systems in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogens is warranted. While these results provide valuable insights, further prospective studies with external validation are needed to confirm whether pathogen-specific factors or injury patterns can refine prognostic models in sepsis. Further research in this study demonstrates that age, respiratory dysfunction, hematological abnormalities, and circulatory impairment were independent risk factors for poor prognosis in patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis, consistent with previous findings [13–15]. Importantly, our study provides novel evidence that among organ dysfunction scoring systems, LODS, OASIS, SIRS, and SAPS III serve as independent prognostic indicators, with LODS emerging as particularly clinically relevant. These hypothesis-generating findings could inform future clinical decision-making by highlighting potential patient-specific risk factors and scoring tools for risk stratification in microbiologically confirmed sepsis. However, prospective multicenter validation is required before these results can be fully implemented as predictive clinical tools. The LODS score, which evaluates six organ systems, is a valuable tool for assessing patient severity in intensive care units and predicting mortality. The comparative analysis of prognostic performance, assessed via DeLong’s test for AUC values, revealed significant differences in predictive accuracy across scoring systems. For 28-day mortality, the LODS score and demonstrated statistically superior discrimination compared to OASIS and SIRS (both p < 0.001), with LODS demonstrating similar utility to SAPS III in this population (p = 0.597). Similarly, for 90-day mortality, LODS significantly outperformed SIRS (p < 0.001), with LODS demonstrating similar utility to SAPS III in this population(p = 0.866). These results suggest that LODS and SAPS III may offer enhanced early risk stratification (28-day) and longer-term outcomes (90-day). Divergent performance underscores the importance of selecting context-appropriate scoring tools based on the clinical endpoint of interest. Given these findings, close monitoring of LODS and SAPS III score trends is recommended for managing such patients. Furthermore, the LODS and SAPS III score has shown strong predictive ability in the prognosis of other critically ill populations [16–20], reinforcing its importance in clinical assessment. Given its established efficacy, the LODS and SAPS III score remains a key prognostic tool in critical care medicine. Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction remains a formidable clinical challenge [21–25]. The pathophysiology involves complex interactions between microbial virulence factors, dysregulated host immunity (including cytokine storms, mitochondrial dysfunction, and coagulopathy), and subsequent tissue hypoxia [26–30]. Our study specifically addresses a critical knowledge gap by focusing on microbiologically-confirmed sepsis—a high-risk subgroup where pathogen-host interactions may amplify organ injury. The identification of modifiable predictors (e.g., early hemodynamic instability, lactate levels, and LODS-quantified organ dysfunction) provides actionable targets for clinicians. These findings enable risk stratification at the intersection of microbial etiology and host response, offering a framework for timely interventions such as tailored antimicrobial therapy, organ support escalation, or immunomodulation in culture-positive sepsis. However, these clinical implications require validation through prospective studies before implementation. Our study of 5,694 patients with microbiologically confirmed sepsis revealed 28-day and 90-day mortality rates of 15.8% and 17.5%, respectively, with organ dysfunction scores (LODS, SAPS III) outperforming inflammatory markers (SIRS) in prognostic accuracy. Notably, pathogen type and infection site did not independently predict outcomes, suggesting that host response patterns—rather than microbial factors alone—drive mortality in this population. For bedside risk stratification, we recommend a two-step approach: (1) Initial rapid triage using the LODS score (requiring only 6 variables) which demonstrated comparable performance to SAPS III (AUC 0.738 vs. 0.734, p = 0.597) but superior to SIRS; followed by (2) Comprehensive evaluation with Model 1 (age + respiratory rate + hemoglobin + lactate + vasopressors + Charlson) for centers lacking informatics support. This balances predictive accuracy (Model 1 AUC 0.746) with clinical feasibility, as it avoids complex score combinations while incorporating readily available clinical variables. The models’ high specificity (0.706–0.765) makes them particularly suitable for identifying high-risk patients requiring ICU escalation. Our findings align with emerging concepts in sepsis subphenotyping, particularly regarding the prognostic value of organ dysfunction patterns (LODS score) in culture-confirmed sepsis. Antcliffe et al. [31] highlight that sepsis heterogeneity necessitates precision medicine approaches, with subphenotypes like the immunosuppressed SRS1 group (characterized by STAT3-mediated granulopoiesis and T-cell exhaustion) showing differential treatment responses. While our study did not perform transcriptomic profiling, the clinical and laboratory predictors we identified (e.g., lactate, vasopressor use, and LODS score) may indirectly reflect these biological endotypes. Our findings underscore the prognostic dominance of host-response markers (e.g., LODS, lactate) over pathogen-specific factors in microbiologically confirmed sepsis, supporting the paradigm of sepsis as a heterogeneous syndrome driven by divergent endotypic responses rather than microbial etiology alone. The consistent predictive performance of organ dysfunction scores across infection sites (abdominal AUC = 0.881; pulmonary AUC = 0.754) suggests these variables may reflect common biological pathways—a hypothesis aligning with Martin-Loeches et al.’s call for endotype-guided stratification [21]. While our models provide clinically actionable risk tools, future studies should explore how these predictors intersect with mechanistically defined subphenotypes (e.g., immunosuppressed or hyperinflammatory endotypes [31]) to enable truly personalized prognosis. This study has several limitations. Firstly, the retrospective design inherently limits causal inference, as temporal relationships between predictor variables and outcomes cannot be definitively established. Although we adjusted for confounders using multivariable regression, unmeasured biases—such as variations in documentation practices (e.g., inconsistent vital sign recording or laboratory sampling frequencies across clinicians)—may persist. Reliance on historical ICU data introduces potential measurement bias, particularly for dynamic parameters like lactate trends or vasopressor dosing, which were captured as worst values within 24 h rather than continuous trajectories. Second, although we adjusted for multiple confounders in our Cox regression models (including comorbidities, treatment intensity, and organ dysfunction scores), residual confounding may persist due to unmeasured variables such as precise antibiotic timing, microbial resistance patterns, or detailed therapeutic strategies. Thirdly, while we included Charlson Comorbidity Index and disease severity scores (e.g., SAPS III, SOFA), these may not fully capture individual variations in disease progression. Fourthly, our findings should be interpreted with caution due to the reliance on a single U.S.-based critical care database (MIMIC-IV), which may limit generalizability to other regions or patient cohorts. Future studies involving multi-center or geographically diverse datasets are needed to externally validate our results. Additionally, this work serves as a hypothesis-generating study, and prospective validation is warranted to confirm clinical applicability. Fifth, we acknowledge that liver function parameters could provide valuable prognostic information; however, due to substantial missing data (> 30% missingness), these variables could not be reliably included in our models—a limitation we have explicitly noted in the manuscript. Last, the exclusion of pathogen-negative sepsis limits the generalizability of our prognostic model. Future studies with standardized diagnostic protocols are needed to clarify whether these groups share similar risk factors. At last, although this study is retrospective, it is currently studying a very large cohort of pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis, so it has great reference value. Patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis had a poor prognosis; the prognosis related to LODS score has a strong predictive value for the short-term and long-term prognosis of patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis.

sections.Background: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection [1]. Studies report that mortality rates remain high, with an average 30-day septic shock mortality of 34.7%, 90-day septic shock mortality of 38.5%, and 90-day sepsis mortality of 32.2% [2]. Consistent with this, multiple studies confirm persistently elevated mortality in sepsis patients [3–5]. Consequently, sepsis carries a poor prognosis with sustained high mortality rates. Sepsis is a heterogeneous disease [6]. According to the latest Sepsis-3.0 definition, sepsis patients include those with confirmed pathogenic microbial infections as well as those with suspected infections but without detected pathogens [1]. Numerous studies have identified pathogenic microorganisms—particularly Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa—as key contributors to infection and elevated mortality [7–9]. Consequently, pathogen-positive sepsis patients are likely to face higher mortality rates and poorer prognoses. This subgroup warrants special clinical attention. However, large cohort studies focusing on pathogen-positive sepsis patients remain scarce. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the clinical characteristics and prognosis of pathogen-positive sepsis, establish a prognostic model for risk assessment, and facilitate early intervention to reduce sepsis-related mortality.
sections.Patients and data description: This retrospective study analyzed adult patients (> 18 years) from the MIMIC-IV v2.2 database (2008–2019) who met sepsis-3.0 criteria (SOFA score ≥ 2 with suspected infection) and had microbiologically confirmed infections (positive bacterial/fungal cultures). In this study utilizing the MIMIC-IV database, culture positivity was strictly defined by clinically significant microbial growth from either sterile sites (blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or sterile body fluids) or non-sterile sites (sputum, urine, or wound cultures) when accompanied by compatible clinical symptoms and subsequent targeted antimicrobial therapy. The database records include standardized culture durations (5 days for bacteria and 30 days for fungi), in accordance with the clinical laboratory protocols at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. Suspected infection required both antibiotic administration (> 48 h) and microbiological culture orders. Only patients with an anticipated ICU survival exceeding 24 h after admission were included. Exclusion criteria comprised culture-negative cases, inter-ICU transfers, incomplete records (missing critical variables such as worst 24-hour ICU vitals/labs), and non-index ICU admissions. The population was obtained from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC IV 2.2) database [10]. The MIMIC IV2.2 database is from populations from 2008 to 2019. The MIMIC-IV database is a publicly available, de-identified critical care dataset from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), containing comprehensive clinical data for over 40,000 ICU patients. The number of patients with a diagnosis of sepsis 3.0 was 25,597, of which 5,694 were sepsis patients who were positive for pathogenic microorganisms. The MIMIC IV v2.2 was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (2001-P001699/14) and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (No. 0403000206). All data were fully de-identified in compliance with ethical regulations, and institutional review board approval was obtained with a waiver of informed consent due to the retrospective use of anonymized records. All studies are based on the Declaration of Helsinki. In this study, we collected baseline data from sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms, including demographic characteristics (age, gender, and comorbidities), infection-related details (site of infection and pathogen species), worst vital signs and laboratory test values within the first 24 h of ICU admission, and prognostic indicators such as vasoactive drug treatment, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), hospitalization duration, ICU length of stay, 28-day mortality, and 90-day mortality. Disease severity was assessed using multiple scoring systems using the worst values within 24 h of ICU admission: the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II) and III, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Logistic Organ Dysfunction System (LODS) score, Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (OASIS), and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria.
sections.Statistical analysis: All continuous variables in this study were skewed and thus presented as the interquartile range (IQR). Group comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables and Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified risk factors associated with 28-day and 90-day mortality in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms. Prognostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement(NRI) along with sensitivity and specificity measures. We employed DeLong’s test to statistically compare the area under the curve (AUC) values between the two models. While our study utilized the entire available cohort from the MIMIC-IV database, we performed a post hoc power calculation based on published literature for similar sepsis prognosis studies. A prior study [11] examining mortality predictors in sepsis reported effect sizes ranging from 1.3 to 2.0 for key variables, including age, organ dysfunction scores, and laboratory markers. Assuming similar effect sizes, a power analysis with α = 0.05 and power = 80% indicated that a minimum sample of 1,200-1,500 patients would be required to detect these clinically meaningful associations. Our final cohort of 5,694 patients, therefore, provides more than adequate power to identify significant predictors while accounting for potential confounders. This sample size also comfortably exceeds the recommended 10–20 events per variable for Cox regression analyses, ensuring robust model development without overfitting. For variables with less than 20% missingness, we employed multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) using predictive mean matching, incorporating all model covariates and outcomes in the imputation model to preserve underlying relationships. Continuous variables were imputed using truncated regression to prevent biologically implausible values, while categorical variables used logistic regression.

sections.The multivariate COX regression analysis:
The variables included in the multivariable Cox regression models (age, respiratory rate, hemoglobin, lactate, vasoactive drug use, SAPS III, Charlson Comorbidity Index, LODS, and SIRS scores) were selected. Age represents physiological reserve deterioration, while lactate and vasoactive agent use directly reflect shock severity. Respiratory rate and hemoglobin levels capture respiratory compensation and oxygen delivery capacity, respectively. The severity scores (SAPS III, LODS, SIRS) quantify organ dysfunction and inflammatory burden - all pathophysiological hallmarks of sepsis. The Charlson Index accounts for baseline mortality risk from comorbidities. These parameters align with current Sepsis-3 definitions and international guidelines for sepsis prognostication. OASIS score was additionally included for 28-day mortality given its validated performance in acute ICU risk stratification. Table 3 demonstrated that age, respiratory rate, hemoglobin level, lactate level, vasoactive drug use, SAPS III score, Charlson Comorbidity Index, LODS score, and SIRS score were independent risk factors for both 28-day and 90-day mortality in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogenic microorganisms. Additionally, the OASIS score was identified as an independent risk factor specifically for 28-day mortality in this patient population. sections.Model 2 performance for 28-day mortality: The predictive performance of Model 2 across clinical subgroups demonstrated consistent discrimination ability for 28-day mortality (Fig. 3A). Among patients with septic shock (n = 2,271, events = 605), the model achieved an AUC of 0.769 (95% CI: 0.747–0.791), slightly higher than in non-shock patients (AUC = 0.746, 95% CI: 0.717–0.774). Notably, the model showed particularly strong discrimination in patients with abdominal infections (AUC = 0.881, 95% CI: 0.824–0.937) and skin/soft tissue infections (AUC = 0.834, 95% CI: 0.766–0.902). For pulmonary infections, performance was maintained in both subgroups (non-pulmonary AUC = 0.803, 95% CI: 0.787–0.820; pulmonary AUC = 0.754, 95% CI: 0.692–0.816). Urinary tract infection subgroups showed comparable AUC values (non-urinary AUC = 0.801; urinary AUC = 0.797), as did catheter-associated infection subgroups (non-catheter AUC = 0.799; catheter AUC = 0.820). sections.Model 4 performance for 90-day mortality: Model 4 maintained robust predictive accuracy for 90-day mortality across all prespecified subgroups (Fig. 3B). Similar to 28-day outcomes, the model performed well in shock patients (AUC = 0.770, 95% CI: 0.748–0.792) and non-shock patients (AUC = 0.734, 95% CI: 0.706–0.762). Discrimination was strongest for abdominal infections (AUC = 0.861, 95% CI: 0.798–0.923) and skin/soft tissue infections (AUC = 0.816, 95% CI: 0.749–0.883). Pulmonary infection subgroups showed slightly reduced but still acceptable performance (non-pulmonary AUC = 0.799; pulmonary AUC = 0.768). The model demonstrated consistent performance between urinary tract infection subgroups (non-urinary AUC = 0.798; urinary AUC = 0.766) and catheter-related infection subgroups (non-catheter AUC = 0.796; catheter AUC = 0.800).
sections.Discussion: The 28-day and 90-day mortality rates in sepsis patients with pathogenic microbiota positivity were 15.8% and 17.5%, respectively. Age, respiratory rate, hemoglobin levels, lactate levels, use of vasoactive drugs, Charlson Comorbidity Index, LODS, OASIS, SIRS, and SAPS III scores were all independent risk factors for both 28-day and 90-day mortality in this patient group (p < 0.001). Additionally, OASIS was specifically identified as an independent risk factor for 28-day mortality. Several studies have reported that sepsis is associated with high morbidity and mortality [4, 11, 12]. This study found that the short-term and long-term mortality rates among patients with sepsis and confirmed pathogenic microorganisms were approximately 20%. Both previous research and this study highlight that sepsis continues to carry a high mortality risk, particularly in patients with microbiologically confirmed infections. However, this study did not identify specific high-mortality pathogenic microorganisms as independent predictors of short- or long-term mortality in this patient population. Instead, mortality may be attributed to multisystem organ damage resulting from the dysregulated inflammatory response triggered by these pathogens. Given these findings, further investigation into multisystem injury patterns and prognostic scoring systems in sepsis patients with confirmed pathogens is warranted. While these results provide valuable insights, further prospective studies with external validation are needed to confirm whether pathogen-specific factors or injury patterns can refine prognostic models in sepsis. Further research in this study demonstrates that age, respiratory dysfunction, hematological abnormalities, and circulatory impairment were independent risk factors for poor prognosis in patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis, consistent with previous findings [13–15]. Importantly, our study provides novel evidence that among organ dysfunction scoring systems, LODS, OASIS, SIRS, and SAPS III serve as independent prognostic indicators, with LODS emerging as particularly clinically relevant. These hypothesis-generating findings could inform future clinical decision-making by highlighting potential patient-specific risk factors and scoring tools for risk stratification in microbiologically confirmed sepsis. However, prospective multicenter validation is required before these results can be fully implemented as predictive clinical tools. The LODS score, which evaluates six organ systems, is a valuable tool for assessing patient severity in intensive care units and predicting mortality. The comparative analysis of prognostic performance, assessed via DeLong’s test for AUC values, revealed significant differences in predictive accuracy across scoring systems. For 28-day mortality, the LODS score and demonstrated statistically superior discrimination compared to OASIS and SIRS (both p < 0.001), with LODS demonstrating similar utility to SAPS III in this population (p = 0.597). Similarly, for 90-day mortality, LODS significantly outperformed SIRS (p < 0.001), with LODS demonstrating similar utility to SAPS III in this population(p = 0.866). These results suggest that LODS and SAPS III may offer enhanced early risk stratification (28-day) and longer-term outcomes (90-day). Divergent performance underscores the importance of selecting context-appropriate scoring tools based on the clinical endpoint of interest. Given these findings, close monitoring of LODS and SAPS III score trends is recommended for managing such patients. Furthermore, the LODS and SAPS III score has shown strong predictive ability in the prognosis of other critically ill populations [16–20], reinforcing its importance in clinical assessment. Given its established efficacy, the LODS and SAPS III score remains a key prognostic tool in critical care medicine. Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction remains a formidable clinical challenge [21–25]. The pathophysiology involves complex interactions between microbial virulence factors, dysregulated host immunity (including cytokine storms, mitochondrial dysfunction, and coagulopathy), and subsequent tissue hypoxia [26–30]. Our study specifically addresses a critical knowledge gap by focusing on microbiologically-confirmed sepsis—a high-risk subgroup where pathogen-host interactions may amplify organ injury. The identification of modifiable predictors (e.g., early hemodynamic instability, lactate levels, and LODS-quantified organ dysfunction) provides actionable targets for clinicians. These findings enable risk stratification at the intersection of microbial etiology and host response, offering a framework for timely interventions such as tailored antimicrobial therapy, organ support escalation, or immunomodulation in culture-positive sepsis. However, these clinical implications require validation through prospective studies before implementation. Our study of 5,694 patients with microbiologically confirmed sepsis revealed 28-day and 90-day mortality rates of 15.8% and 17.5%, respectively, with organ dysfunction scores (LODS, SAPS III) outperforming inflammatory markers (SIRS) in prognostic accuracy. Notably, pathogen type and infection site did not independently predict outcomes, suggesting that host response patterns—rather than microbial factors alone—drive mortality in this population. For bedside risk stratification, we recommend a two-step approach: (1) Initial rapid triage using the LODS score (requiring only 6 variables) which demonstrated comparable performance to SAPS III (AUC 0.738 vs. 0.734, p = 0.597) but superior to SIRS; followed by (2) Comprehensive evaluation with Model 1 (age + respiratory rate + hemoglobin + lactate + vasopressors + Charlson) for centers lacking informatics support. This balances predictive accuracy (Model 1 AUC 0.746) with clinical feasibility, as it avoids complex score combinations while incorporating readily available clinical variables. The models’ high specificity (0.706–0.765) makes them particularly suitable for identifying high-risk patients requiring ICU escalation. Our findings align with emerging concepts in sepsis subphenotyping, particularly regarding the prognostic value of organ dysfunction patterns (LODS score) in culture-confirmed sepsis. Antcliffe et al. [31] highlight that sepsis heterogeneity necessitates precision medicine approaches, with subphenotypes like the immunosuppressed SRS1 group (characterized by STAT3-mediated granulopoiesis and T-cell exhaustion) showing differential treatment responses. While our study did not perform transcriptomic profiling, the clinical and laboratory predictors we identified (e.g., lactate, vasopressor use, and LODS score) may indirectly reflect these biological endotypes. Our findings underscore the prognostic dominance of host-response markers (e.g., LODS, lactate) over pathogen-specific factors in microbiologically confirmed sepsis, supporting the paradigm of sepsis as a heterogeneous syndrome driven by divergent endotypic responses rather than microbial etiology alone. The consistent predictive performance of organ dysfunction scores across infection sites (abdominal AUC = 0.881; pulmonary AUC = 0.754) suggests these variables may reflect common biological pathways—a hypothesis aligning with Martin-Loeches et al.’s call for endotype-guided stratification [21]. While our models provide clinically actionable risk tools, future studies should explore how these predictors intersect with mechanistically defined subphenotypes (e.g., immunosuppressed or hyperinflammatory endotypes [31]) to enable truly personalized prognosis. This study has several limitations. Firstly, the retrospective design inherently limits causal inference, as temporal relationships between predictor variables and outcomes cannot be definitively established. Although we adjusted for confounders using multivariable regression, unmeasured biases—such as variations in documentation practices (e.g., inconsistent vital sign recording or laboratory sampling frequencies across clinicians)—may persist. Reliance on historical ICU data introduces potential measurement bias, particularly for dynamic parameters like lactate trends or vasopressor dosing, which were captured as worst values within 24 h rather than continuous trajectories. Second, although we adjusted for multiple confounders in our Cox regression models (including comorbidities, treatment intensity, and organ dysfunction scores), residual confounding may persist due to unmeasured variables such as precise antibiotic timing, microbial resistance patterns, or detailed therapeutic strategies. Thirdly, while we included Charlson Comorbidity Index and disease severity scores (e.g., SAPS III, SOFA), these may not fully capture individual variations in disease progression. Fourthly, our findings should be interpreted with caution due to the reliance on a single U.S.-based critical care database (MIMIC-IV), which may limit generalizability to other regions or patient cohorts. Future studies involving multi-center or geographically diverse datasets are needed to externally validate our results. Additionally, this work serves as a hypothesis-generating study, and prospective validation is warranted to confirm clinical applicability. Fifth, we acknowledge that liver function parameters could provide valuable prognostic information; however, due to substantial missing data (> 30% missingness), these variables could not be reliably included in our models—a limitation we have explicitly noted in the manuscript. Last, the exclusion of pathogen-negative sepsis limits the generalizability of our prognostic model. Future studies with standardized diagnostic protocols are needed to clarify whether these groups share similar risk factors. At last, although this study is retrospective, it is currently studying a very large cohort of pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis, so it has great reference value.
sections.Conclusion: Patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis had a poor prognosis; the prognosis related to LODS score has a strong predictive value for the short-term and long-term prognosis of patients with pathogenic microorganism-positive sepsis.
